[...] Examples like ˈkam.ni.bak 'friend' show that the stress never moves to the final syllable, even when the syllable is heavy. Patterns where the final syllable is stressed are possible though, because prefixes are not part of the stress domain. new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress is initial by default; if the word contains closed (heavy) syllables, main stress falls on the rightmost closed syllable that is not word-final (i.e. stress may move rightward only as far as the penult); word-final syllables are never stressed within the stem+suffix domain. Prefixes (possessive a-, u-, reduplicative prefixes) are outside the stress domain, so prefixed monosyllabic stems surface with final stress (a.ˈpaŋ 'my house').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Author states it is hard to tell whether there is secondary stress; none detected even in five-syllable words. Secondary stress is clearly audible in compounds, on the first syllable of the second member (main stress stays on the first syllable of the whole compound, and such compounds may override the ban on final stress, e.g. ˈko.len.ˌluŋ). In inflected verb forms secondary stress can appear on the verb stem (ˌndum.men.cu.ˈŋan.na).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Lexicalized monosyllabic kin terms with possessive prefix take initial stress on the prefix (ˈa.mum 'grandmother') but revert when the prefix changes (u.ˈmum); (ii) nominalizing clitics =na/=ha, unlike other clitics, count as part of the verb's stress domain; (iii) triplicated ideophonic adverbs have lengthened, stressed final syllable ([se.re.ˈreː] 'drizzling'); (iv) in noun-verb complex predicates and co-compounds each component carries its own stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = stem plus suffixes; prefixes and phrase-level clitics (case, discourse markers) are excluded and do not affect stress. Description based on the Tumok village dialect; impressionistic (no instrumental study).
new_statements.identity_note: Schackow (2015) describes the Tumok (Nepali: Tamaphok) village dialect of Yakkha, Sankhuwa Sabha district, eastern Nepal; the author notes at least four Yakkha dialects. Glottocode yakk1236 (ISO ybh) is the language-level code; no separate dialect glottocode identified.

The catalog record for Yakkha has an empty rule field, so this source supplies the placement: default initial, moved to the last non-final closed syllable (weight-sensitive, initial default, rightward to closed syllables, final excluded). The full read adds the secondary-stress observations, the kin-term prefix exception, the nominalizer-in-domain detail and the triplicated-adverb final-stress exception, all compatible with the existing reading.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress is on the first syllable by default; if the word contains closed (heavy) syllables, main stress moves to the last closed syllable that is not word-final (i.e. the rightmost non-final heavy syllable, never beyond the penult). Word-final syllables are never stressed even when heavy. The stress domain is stem plus suffixes: possessive and reduplicative prefixes and phrasal clitics (case, discourse clitics) lie outside it, so a prefix + monosyllabic stem surfaces as apparently final-stressed (a.ˈpaŋ ‘my house’); the nominalizers =na/=ha attached to verbs do count as part of the domain.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 61: 'It is hard to tell whether there is secondary stress. Even in words with five syllables, like in (14b), no secondary stress could be detected. Secondary stress was clearly audible in compounds such as those shown in Table 3.12. It is found on the first syllable of the second part of the compound, while the main stress remains on the first syllable of the whole compound. Such compounds may override the general restriction against stress on word-final syllables. In inflected verb forms, secondary stress can be found on the verbal stem, e.g., in ˌndum.men.cu.ˈŋan.na'
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Lexicalized monosyllabic kin terms with the 1sg possessive prefix a- take stress on the prefix (ˈa.mum ‘grandmother’, ˈa.pum, ˈa.na, ˈa.phu; also ˈu.wa ‘liquid’), but replacing the prefix restores the expected pattern (u.ˈmum), p. 59. (b) Reduplicated adjectives/adverbs are stressed on the second syllable because the reduplicant is a prefix outside the domain (pha.ˈphap, son.ˈson), pp. 59-60. (c) Nominalizers =na/=ha on verbs are inside the stress domain unlike other clitics, p. 61. (d) 'one exception to the stress rules': triplicated ideophonic adverbs with lengthened final vowel are always stressed on the last syllable ([se.re.ˈreː] ‘drizzling’, [hi.wi.ˈwiː]), p. 61. (e) Compounds may carry secondary stress on a word-final syllable, p. 61. (f) Ch. 5-6 note co-compounds and noun-verb predicates (ˈsak.ˈtuk.ma) each carry their own stress, i.e. two stress domains.
new_statements.identity_note: Schackow 2015 explicitly documents the Tumok dialect of Yakkha (section 2.4.1 'Dialectal variation', p. 34: 'The variety documented here is spoken in Tumok village and surrounding areas, e.g., in Salle'; section 2.1: 'The focus of this work is on the Tumok dialect'). She names at least three further dialects (Dandagaun, Ankhinbhuin, Kharang) but gives no stress data for them.
